one_liner: Header-only liburing adapter for stdexec (std::execution) senders; beats Asio's io_uring backend on loopback TCP ping-pong.
what_it_does: Wraps liburing's io_uring_prep_* calls as stdexec senders (async_accept, async_read, async_write, async_connect, async_wait, async_sigwait and more), so socket and file I/O compose with then/let_value/when_any, C++20 coroutines, async_scope and stop tokens. You create one io_uring_exec, get its scheduler, and call run() from as many threads as you like. It is not a drop-in for Asio: there are no socket, buffer or completion-token types, just raw file descriptors and sender algorithms. make_uring_sender_v<io_uring_prep_X> turns any other prep function into a sender in one line.
how_it_is_fast: Each thread that calls run() lazily gets its own thread-local io_uring ring, created with IORING_SETUP_SINGLE_ISSUER and IORING_SETUP_COOP_TASKRUN, and all rings share one kernel worker pool through IORING_SETUP_ATTACH_WQ. Operation states are immovable and intrusive, with a per-object vtable for type erasure, and the CQE user_data points straight at them, so the library itself does no per-I/O heap allocation. Work scheduled from other threads goes through lock-free CAS intrusive queues split into 16 buckets that run threads drain by round-robin plus random pick. The default run loop submits without blocking, harvests completions in batches with io_uring_peek_batch_cqe (64 per batch, up to 512 per step) and calls yield() when idle instead of sleeping in the kernel. The author gives no explanation of why this beats Asio.
when_to_use: Your code base already uses stdexec/P2300 senders and you want Linux socket or file I/O as composable senders with stop-token cancellation and when_any timeouts.
Many concurrent TCP connections (1,000-100,000) served by several threads on one box. The author's newer table has it beating Asio epoll there, e.g. 8 threads/10,000 sessions 6.662 vs 2.118 GiB/s.
A single-threaded event loop: at 1 thread it beat both Asio backends at every session count in the author's table (e.g. 100 sessions: 4.026 vs 3.600 io_uring, 3.052 epoll GiB/s).
You can give the event loop dedicated cores, because the default run loop polls and yields rather than blocking.
As a small, readable reference (about 1,600 lines of headers) for mapping io_uring onto sender/receiver before writing your own.
when_not_to_use: Few connections spread over several threads. In 5 of the 6 rows with 10-100 sessions and 2-8 threads, Asio's default epoll backend was 1.4-3.2x faster in the author's own table (4 threads/100 sessions: 8.744 vs 3.226 GiB/s), and the author says io_uring cannot beat epoll on the current kernel.

Production services that need a maintained dependency: the README calls it effectively archived since 2025, there is one author, the repo has only two test files and no CI config, and the build follows stdexec main, whose upstream changes have broken compilation (issue #2, the 2026-05 fix commit, a ~10x compile-time regression noted for ping_when_any).
You need TLS, DNS or higher-level socket types. The API is raw file descriptors, and the author says in issue #3 that async OpenSSL is out of scope (workarounds: poll-based SSL or kTLS).
You want advanced io_uring features: the sender list has no multishot accept/recv, provided buffer rings, registered files/buffers or zero-copy send.

Non-Linux targets, kernels older than about 6.1 (the recommended minimum), or environments where io_uring is disabled. Also workloads that cancel every I/O, since per-operation cancellation adds overhead according to the benchmarks README.

integration.dependencies: stdexec (NVIDIA, tracked at main), liburing (link -luring, recent enough for io_uring_prep_futex_wait/bind), pthread; Asio only for the comparison benchmark
integration.min_toolchain: C++20; benchmarked with GCC 13.2; the benchmarks README says Clang also works (there is a clang-19 workaround commit)
integration.platforms: Linux only (io_uring), kernel 6.1+ recommended; architecture support not documented (benchmarked on x86-64 AMD 5800H)
integration.thread_safety: io_uring_exec is documented as MT-safe: any number of threads may call run() on one instance and schedule work from any thread. Each run thread owns a thread-local ring.

gotchas: The default run() never blocks in the kernel. It calls io_uring_submit without waiting, peeks the CQ and calls std::this_thread::yield() when nothing moved, so each run thread keeps a core busy even when idle. run_policy{.waitable=true} switches to io_uring_submit_and_wait.

An I/O sender submits its SQE to the thread-local ring of whichever thread calls start(). Hop onto the scheduler first (stdexec::schedule or starts_on, as every example does), or the operation sits in a ring that no run() loop drains.

Thread-local rings are keyed by the io_uring_exec constructor's call site through a template lambda parameter. The header warns that constructing it repeatedly at one site (e.g. in a loop) reuses the same per-thread ring, so treat it as a long-lived singleton. The constructor is noexcept, but ring setup throws std::system_error on failure, which means std::terminate if io_uring is unavailable.

async_read/async_write default to offset 0, so on a seekable file every call hits byte 0 unless you pass an offset. Errors arrive as set_error(exception_ptr to std::system_error), and -ECANCELED arrives as set_stopped.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick uring_exec when you specifically want io_uring exposed as std::execution senders. For a maintained C++20-coroutine io_uring runtime that aims to cover most io_uring features and also posts wins over epoll and Asio, Condy is the safer choice. At low connection counts, stock Asio on epoll (or PhotonLibOS, which edges out boost::asio in its own ping-pong) is faster than uring_exec according to the author's own data.
verified_claims_summary: Loopback TCP ping-pong on one AMD 5800H box (Linux 6.4.8, GCC 13.2 -O3, 16 KiB blocks, 5 s): a uring_exec echo server beat an Asio coroutine echo server built with ASIO_HAS_IO_URING and ASIO_DISABLE_EPOLL by 1.27x-3.46x across 2/4/8 threads and 10/100/1000 sessions (e.g. 4 threads/1000 sessions: 4.411 vs 1.275 GiB/s). The client was uring_exec's own ping in both cases, and there was one run per cell with no variance reported. A newer 10 s table in benchmarks/README adds Asio on epoll, which beats uring_exec at 10-100 sessions with 2+ threads.
status_note: The author declares it effectively archived since 2025 (the last commit, 2026-05-01, only follows stdexec API renames); it is header-only and MPL-2.0, so it is easy to vendor, but you inherit stdexec churn yourself.
